To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the average excess energy intake responsible for the obesity increase between 1988 and 1994 and 2000 in the US corresponds to 100 calories/day, (2) this energy can be burned by 30–60 min/day of walking at slow or brisk pace, (3) a new commuter light rail transit in North Carolina provoked an 18% decrease in BMI in the users compared to the nonusers, corresponding to an excess energy expenditure of 107 calories/day.

(i) the LRT commuters lost 6.5 lb of weight in 7 months; (ii) this weight loss corresponds to a daily excess energy expenditure of 107 kcal/day, which in turn corresponds to an average of 30 min/day spent in brisk walking.

(a) The introduction of a new light rail transit in North Carolina was followed by a significant reduction in the average body mass index of people who started commuting to work on the new transit compared to those who did not.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the introduction of the new light-rail commuter train (LRT) on the weight of its passengers.
the role that public transportation may play in addressing two major public health problems, global warming and obesity (Morabia et al. 2010).
the impact of the introduction of a LRT system on the weight of its users.

the use of public transportation is an effective and practical way to reduce the risk of obesity.

(i) the obesity epidemic is a major public health problem, (ii) physical inactivity is one of its major causes, (iii) public transportation is a promising way to increase physical activity, and (iv) more research is needed on this topic.
